title: Annotatio II §.IV: Chrysostom & Theodoret — bread remains after sanctification (Burnet / Picherellus)
pass_a_gloss: Several such places, and altogether the same ones, the Most Reverend Burnet brings into the middle in his Exposition of the 39 Articles of the Anglican Church p. 330, and the most learned Picherellus Opuscula Theologica p. 176 — namely Chrysostom writing to the monk Caesarius: Just as before the bread is sanctified we name it bread: but when divine grace sanctifies it, the priest mediating, it is freed indeed from the appellation of bread, yet is counted worthy of the appellation of the Lord’s body, and the signature of bread remained in it. And Theodoret speaking thus in the Dialogue: Nor do the mystical signs after sanctification withdraw from their nature: For they remain in the prior substance and figure and form and can be seen and touched, and are bread &c.; but they are understood as what they are and are believed, in the second Dialogue.
pass_b_english: Burnet (39 Articles p. 330) and Picherellus (Opusc. Theol. p. 176) stack the same loci.
Chrysostom to Caesarius: after sanctification the bread is worthy of the Lord’s-body name, yet the bread-signature remains.
Theodoret’s Dialogue II: the mystical signs keep prior substance, figure, and form — still bread to sight and touch, understood as believed.
source_text: Loca hujusmodi aliquot, eademque omnino, in medium adducunt Reverendissimus Burnetus in Expositione 39. articulorum Ecclesiæ Anglicanæ pag. 330. & doctissimus Picherellus Opuscula Theol. p. 176, Chrysostomi scil. ad Cæsareum Monachum scribentis: Sicut antequam sanctificatur panis, panem nominamus: Divina autem illum sanctificante gratiâ, mediante sacerdote, liberatus est quidem ab appellatione panis, dignus autem habitus est Dominici corporis appellatione, & signatura panis in ipso permanfit. THEODORETI in Dialogo ita loquentis: Neque signa mystica post sanctificationem recedunt à sua natura: Manent enim in priore substantia & figura & forma & videri & tangi possunt, suntque panis &c. intelliguntur autem ea quæ sunt & creduntur, Dialogo secundo.
